written.q: Explain why timers and counters are implemented as peripherals, and describe how an 8-bit timer measures time and how it counts events.
written.a: Doing timing and counting in software ties up the small CPU. A timer peripheral increments its TCNT register on each clock pulse from the oscillator (optionally through a prescaler), counts 0 to 255 and overflows to 0, setting TOV in TIFR. Because the clock frequency is known, elapsed time = N×(B−A)/f. If a pulse source such as a button or sensor is connected to the Tn pin (CS bits 110 or 111) the same hardware counts events.

written.q: Calculate the initial value of a 16-bit timer to overflow every 100 ms with F_CPU = 16 MHz, and write the code to toggle PB5 using the overflow interrupt.
written.a:
Choose prescale 64: tick 4 µs, n = 0.1/4 µs = 25 000, initial = 65 535 − 25 000 + 1 = 40 536.

DDRB |= (1<<DDB5);
TCCR1B |= (1<<CS11)|(1<<CS10);   // /64
TCNT1 = 40536;
TIMSK1 |= (1<<TOIE1); sei();
while(1){}
ISR(TIMER1_OVF_vect){ PORTB ^= (1<<PORTB5); TCNT1 = 40536; }

written.q: Describe the reaction timer design and explain how the random waiting time and the reaction time are obtained.
written.a: Ready and react buttons (pull-ups) on PD2 and PD3, blue, green, orange and red LEDs on PB0 to PB3. While waiting for ready, Timer0 free-runs; srand(TCNT0) at the press gives a fairly random seed (or the ADC of a floating pin). Timer1 with prescale 1024 and initial value 49 911 overflows every second; the firmware waits 1 + rand() % 10 overflows, lights the blue LED, then counts overflows until react is pressed. 0 s → green, 1 s → orange, 2 s or more → red.

written.q: What is the W1C flag clearing convention and why is it used?
written.a: Write one to clear: a flag such as TOVn is cleared by writing a 1 to its bit. Writing a mask that has a single 1 clears only that flag and leaves other flags (which also live in TIFRn) untouched; a read-modify-write to clear by writing 0 could clear flags set in between.
